overview.text: Velocity describes how an object's position changes over time. Average velocity is displacement—the vector from the starting position to the ending position—divided by elapsed time, not total path length divided by time. Because velocity is a vector, it includes both magnitude and direction; speed is its magnitude and does not specify direction. Instantaneous velocity describes motion at a particular moment. Along a curved path, its direction is tangent to the path. Velocity is commonly measured in meters per second (m/s), and a change in either speed or direction changes velocity.

key_facts.text: Average velocity equals displacement divided by elapsed time: v_avg = Δx/Δt.
Velocity is a vector, so a complete description includes direction; speed is scalar and gives only magnitude.
Average velocity can be zero on a round trip even when the traveler covers a nonzero distance, because the final position matches the starting position.
Instantaneous velocity describes motion at a specific moment; it equals average velocity over an interval when velocity is constant.
For motion along a curved path, the instantaneous velocity vector points tangent to the path.
